title: Decoder- and Noise-Aware Optimization Framework for Clifford-Deformed Quantum Error-Correcting Codes
authors: Julius Rye Bønnelykke, Benjamin Joecker, Peter Krogstrup, Vincent Philippe Michal, Mark Kamper Svendsen
abstract: Practical fault-tolerant quantum computing requires qubit-efficient quantum error correction (QEC). Clifford deformations (CDs) modify the stabilizers of a QEC code to lower its logical error rate at no additional resource cost. However, the number of possible CDs grows exponentially with the number of qubits, making exhaustive search infeasible beyond small codes. In this work, we further show that under circuit level noise the optimal CD depends strongly on both the noise model and decoder. To make systematic CD optimization possible, we introduce Evolution-Based Best-arm Identification (EBBI), a shot-efficient search algorithm that treats the circuit, noise model and decoder as a black box. We benchmark EBBI's performance on the rotated surface code, under two strongly $Z$-biased circuit-level noise models with the PyMatching decoder. At distance 3, EBBI finds the optimal CD using up to $\sim 1100\times$ fewer shots than random search. At distance 5, when run at the target error rate, the median EBBI run converges to the CDs we believe to be optimal, while random search never converges. Under a $Z$-biased SI1000-like noise model, EBBI discovers a new CD, the B-XZZX code, which we generalized to larger distances. It differs from XZZX on only a fraction $\mathcal{O}(d^{-1})$ of the qubits at code distance $d$, yet its relative advantage grows from $\approx 5\%$ at $d = 3$ to $\approx 12\%$ at $d = 11$. We thus show that the B-XZZX pattern found by EBBI can be systematically scaled to larger code distances. Our work represents a first step towards scalable CD optimization for general QEC codes.
summary: This work presents a novel optimization framework, EBBI, to efficiently search for the best Clifford Deformations for Quantum Error-Correcting Codes. By treating the noise and decoding process as a black box, EBBI significantly outperforms random search in finding CDs that minimize logical errors under realistic circuit-level noise. This advances the field toward scalable, practical fault-tolerant quantum computation.
main_problem: The core problem is finding the optimal Clifford Deformation (CD) for Quantum Error-Correcting Codes (QEC) to minimize the logical error rate, as exhaustive search over the exponentially growing space of CDs is infeasible.
main_result: The proposed algorithm, EBBI, successfully identifies near-optimal CDs with vastly fewer shots than random search, and it discovered a new, systematically scalable CD pattern (B-XZZX) with a measurable advantage over existing codes.
method: The authors introduce Evolution-Based Best-arm Identification (EBBI), a shot-efficient search algorithm that treats the entire optimization process (circuit, noise, decoder) as a black box, combining evolutionary search principles with statistical sampling.
model_or_system: The study focuses on QEC codes, specifically benchmarking on the surface code, and analyzing performance under realistic circuit-level noise models (e.g., Z-biased noise).
key_observables: Logical error rate ($P_L$), number of shots required for optimization, and the relative performance advantage of the discovered CD.
important_parameters: Code distance ($d$), physical error rate ($p$), and the specific noise model (e.g., SI1000-like).
main_assumptions: The success of the search relies on the assumption that small changes in CD patterns result in similar logical error rates, allowing the search to be guided effectively.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the EBBI search process (Initialization, Sampling, Pruning) and compare the PL rankings of various CDs under different noise models and decoders, showing EBBI's superior convergence.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the difficulty of CD optimization, then details the EBBI algorithm, benchmarks its performance on the surface code using specific noise models, and concludes by demonstrating the scalability and novelty of the discovered optimal CD patterns.
why_interesting: The development of EBBI provides a scalable, data-driven methodology for optimizing QEC codes, moving beyond brute-force searches to tackle complex, high-dimensional optimization problems in quantum information.
